hints.junior: The flag resolves 700ms after the page painted, and the banner it inserts pushes the paragraph a reader's already scrolled to right out from under them.
hints.mid: A flag gated on a network response genuinely has two render states — pre-flag and post-flag — and the transition between them is a real, visible layout event.
hints.staff: It's not about the flag being slow — a flag resolved in 50ms still shifts layout if the browser already painted around the pre-flag content.

hints.junior: Click "Simulate page load" in each mode and watch whether the banner is there from frame one or pops in and pushes content down.
hints.mid: Broken mode measures the actual inserted banner height from the DOM after the delay — fixed mode never has anything to measure because nothing moves.
hints.staff: The shift number in broken mode isn't a fixed constant — it's read from getBoundingClientRect after insertion, the same way a real CLS score is computed from actual element movement.

hints.junior: Resolve the flag on the server so the client's first paint already reflects the right variant — there's nothing left to swap in later.
hints.mid: Reserving space for the flagged content, a skeleton sized to match, keeps the box from moving even when what's inside it swaps in late.
hints.staff: Server-side evaluation collapses two round trips into one, removing the client-side transition entirely rather than just making it faster.

hints.junior: A 50ms flag fetch can still cause a visible jump if the browser already painted before it resolved — speed alone doesn't fix that.
hints.mid: A skeleton sized to the eventual banner is a legitimate middle-ground fix when moving evaluation server-side genuinely isn't an option yet.
hints.staff: Bucketing flags are usually safe to resolve server-side from a hashed user ID — killswitch flags need to stay pollable, so they need additive UI instead.

sections.junior: Today's case is about a feature flag that resolves after the page already painted, and the visible jump that happens when its content swaps in mid-read.
sections.mid: Any flag gated on a network response has two real render states, before and after it resolves, and the transition between them is a genuine layout event a reader can see.
sections.staff: The flicker isn't really about the flag being slow. It's about the coupling between when the flag resolves and when the browser has already committed to a layout.

sections.junior: The strongest fix is resolving the flag on the server, before the page is even sent to the browser, so there's nothing left to swap in later.
sections.mid: When the flag has to resolve on the client, reserving space for it ahead of time means the content changes, but nothing else on the page has to move.
sections.staff: Server-side evaluation collapses two round trips into one, so the browser's very first render is already the correct one.

sections.junior: Try simulating a page load in both modes, and watch what happens to the paragraph below the banner.
sections.mid: Broken mode waits, then inserts the banner and measures how far everything below it actually moved.
sections.staff: Fixed mode isn't just a faster version of the same delay, the banner is part of the very first paint, so there's no transition to measure at all.

sections.junior: Resolve the flag before the page renders, or fast enough that nothing has painted yet, so there's nothing to visibly swap in later.
sections.mid: Move flag evaluation onto the server or into edge middleware so the browser's first render is already correct.
sections.staff: Killswitch flags that must stay live client-side need additive UI that never replaces what the reader is already looking at.
